analysis.one_liner: Makes it illegal to sell tobacco products to anyone under 21.
analysis.headline: The bill to raise the tobacco sale age to 21 never got a committee vote or a floor vote before Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The Tobacco to 21 Act would have made it illegal nationwide to sell or distribute any tobacco product — cigarettes, cigars, smokeless tobacco, and e-cigarettes — to anyone under 21, and put the Department of Health and Human Services in charge of enforcement through retailer inspections, undercover compliance checks, and penalties. The bill's own findings cite a National Academy of Medicine estimate that a national Tobacco 21 law would eventually cut smoking rates by about 12% and prevent roughly 223,000 premature deaths among people born between 2000 and 2019 [S3]. It was introduced in November 2017, referred to the Senate Commerce Committee, and died there without a vote [S1] [S5].
analysis.who_benefits: Young people, most directly: about 95% of adult smokers start before 21, and the bill's findings argue that cutting off sales at 21 targets the exact ages (18 to 21) when experimental smoking turns into daily use [S3]. The findings also cite public opinion — three-quarters of Americans, including 7 in 10 smokers, favored raising the sale age to 21 [S3]. Families and the health care system would also benefit from reduced tobacco-related illness and its estimated $170 billion in annual direct medical costs [S3].

how_it_helps.text: Prohibits selling or giving any tobacco product — including e-cigarettes — to anyone under 21, nationwide.
Directs HHS to enforce the ban through undercover compliance checks, retailer inspections, enforcement actions, and ID-check requirements for retailers.

The bill's findings cite the National Academy of Medicine's estimate that a national Tobacco 21 law would reduce smoking prevalence by 12% over time and prevent 223,000 premature deaths, including 50,000 lung cancer deaths, among those born between 2000 and 2019.
Lets states and cities keep or adopt stricter local tobacco age laws, so the national floor does not override tougher local rules.

analysis.who_pays: Tobacco manufacturers would lose the 18-to-20-year-old customer group permanently, and retailers that sell tobacco — convenience stores, gas stations, and vape shops — would bear new ID-check requirements, inspection risk, and federal penalties under the Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act if they sold to underage buyers [S2] [S3].

drawbacks.text: The ban covers legal adults aged 18 to 20, who can vote and serve in the military; an 18-year-old could legally enlist but not legally buy a cigarette under this bill.
Retailers would face new compliance duties — required ID checks, inspections, undercover checks, and federal penalties for violations — costs that fall hardest on small shops.
The bill creates a new federal enforcement program at HHS, which requires appropriations and federal administrative effort to actually carry out.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The public health case was strong by the bill's own evidence: nearly all adult smokers start before 21, an independent National Academy of Medicine review projected hundreds of thousands of premature deaths prevented, and three-quarters of the public supported the change [S3]. The real costs are borne narrowly by tobacco sellers and are the standard costs of enforcing an age-restriction law. The main honest objection is the treatment of 18-to-20-year-old adults, which is a values question rather than a design flaw.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the Senate Commerce Committee, where it sat with no hearing, no markup, and no vote before the 115th Congress ended.

narrative.text: Sen. Brian Schatz introduced the Tobacco to 21 Act on November 8, 2017, joined by 11 Democratic cosponsors.
The bill was read twice and referred to the Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation the same day — the only action recorded in its history.
No further action appears in the record: the committee never reported the bill and the Senate never voted on it before the 115th Congress ended in January 2019.
A national tobacco sale age of 21 did not take effect until late 2019, after this bill's Congress had ended.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Tobacco manufacturers and retailers kept their legal ability to sell to 18-to-20-year-olds for two more years, and the public did not get the reductions in youth smoking the bill was written to deliver. A national Tobacco 21 law only arrived through separate legislation after this Congress ended.

for.name: Sen. Brian Schatz
for.role: U.S. Senator from Hawaii; bill sponsor
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Tobacco to 21 Act and brought 11 Senate cosponsors onto it.

for.name: 11 Senate Democrats
for.role: Cosponsors (Durbin, Markey, Whitehouse, Reed, Brown, Gillibrand, Warren, Hirono, Blumenthal, Feinstein, Franken)

against.name: Senate Commerce Committee leadership
against.role: Chair, Senate Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a hearing or markup on the bill, leaving it in committee without a vote for the rest of the Congress.

against.name: Tobacco industry
against.role: Manufacturers and retailers of tobacco products
against.what_they_did: The bill's own findings state the industry continues to challenge tobacco control measures in court, manipulate products to evade regulations, and spend billions on marketing; industry groups lobbied against federal and state Tobacco 21 proposals as they moved in this period.

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever taken, so the party split on the merits is unknown; sponsorship was entirely Democratic, while the bill's findings cite three-quarters public support, including 7 in 10 smokers [S3] [S4].

industries.note: The bill permanently removes 18-to-20-year-olds from their customer base and covers e-cigarettes, the fastest-growing youth product. Its findings document the industry's history of challenging tobacco control measures and spending billions on youth-oriented marketing [S3].

industries.industry: Tobacco retailers (convenience stores, gas stations, vape shops)
industries.note: Retailers lose sales to young adult customers and take on ID-check mandates, inspections, and federal penalties under the Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act [S2] [S3].

The bill's findings cite roughly $170 billion a year in direct medical costs from tobacco use; reducing smoking initiation reduces those costs over time, a benefit insurers and public programs share with the public [S3].
